newsitem.title: USA: Former U.S. defence chiefs back chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Former U.S. defence chiefs back chemical treaty.

text.p: Former U.S. Defence Secretaries William Perry, Harold Brown and Eliott Richardson on Thursday urged the Senate to ratify a controversial international treaty outlawing chemical weapons.

Army General John Shalikashvilki, chairman of the Pentagon Joint Chiefs of Staff, also reiterated the support of the nation's top military officers for the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) as the Senate moved nearer to a vote on the treaty.

"We firmly believe that U.S. ratification of the CWC (Chemical Weapons Convention) will contribute significantly to the security interests of the United States and safety of our armed forces," Perry, Brown and Richardson said in a brief statement released by the Pentagon.
They joined current Defence Secretary William Cohen in backing the treaty.

"In light of the decision under President Reagan to get rid of the vast majority of U.S. chemical weapons stockpiles, it is in our interests to require other nations to do the same," the statement said.
President Bill Clinton is pushing for Senate approval of the convention before April 29, when it enters into force, with or without the United States.
The treaty, signed by 161 nations and ratified by 70, bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. Its approval requires a two-third majority of the Senate.
Four other former defence secretaries -- Dick Cheney, Caspar Weinberger, James Schlesinger and Donald Rumsfeld -- have urged the Senate to refuse to ratify the CWC, calling it unenforceable.
But Shalikashvili said on Thursday that despite drawbacks in the treaty, it would leave the United States on "a level playing field" with other nations.
"Our troops will be safer with the convention than without it," Shalikashvili he told reporters in an appearance in the Pentagon press room to pressure the Senate.

He said the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other U.S. military commanders around the world realised that there were "rogue states" that would not sign up to the treaty, but that export rules in the document would make it harder for them to obtain components for chemical arms.

Shalikashvili also reiterated that despite a major cutback in U.S. chemical arms, the nation will remain able to launch an "overwhelming and devastating response" to any use of chemical arms against the United States or its forces.
"We do not exclude any capabiliuty that is at our disposal," the general replied when asked if nuclear weapons might be used in such a response.
